findings.text: Documents already available in other departmental systems - such as property tax payment (visible online) and NOC/registry details - are still demanded afresh for Building Plan Approval.
Remarks returned on BPA files are frequently generic or unexplained (e.g. repeated 'please check again'), with no officer held accountable and no reason recorded.
Participants report an officer-level SLA of thirty days for BPA, but individual files routinely sit three to four days at each desk as they move through multiple officers.

Authorised architects' approval powers - previously covering both residential and commercial plots up to a prescribed area for ten to twelve years - were narrowed to residential-only through an undocumented software change conveyed verbally, with no gazette notification; the term 'public at large' used in the related notification is undefined.

A participant's demand draft, prepared over five to six days at a Gurugram head office, was rejected at submission because the department said DDs were no longer accepted, despite the portal showing it as a payment option.
Compliance requirements such as compulsory soil testing can require plan changes and added cost before approval, borne entirely by the owner, who must also engage an architect regardless.
There is no provision in policy for obtaining building permission for an existing fort or heritage site.
Deemed approval after thirty days is understood by applicants in principle, but a return or comment arriving close to the deadline restarts the clock in practice.

Participants list multiple levies collected on the same plot - construction, water, development and labour welfare charges - and ask why several are collected again, without clarity on whether these duplicate the ABPAS-generated statutory fee.

In rural areas and Tier III/IV cities the municipal officer is often not technical and simply forwards files to the town and country planning office, while the applicant is asked to pay development-permission and other charges in the meantime.

Approval authority is split by plot size (building officer vs. city planner), but data verification for even very small plots now sits with the city planner, separating the officer who approves from the one who verifies.
Layout and colony details are demanded again even where the town and country planning office has already approved the layout.
Scanned documents submitted online are subsequently asked for again in hard copy, and software scrutiny is followed by a separate round of manual scrutiny.
Queries are raised one at a time rather than together, so each return restarts the applicant's wait even where the rest of the file is in order.

Multiple departments and approval levels under one nominal authority, with poor coordination between offices of the same department, and weak technical capacity in smaller municipal bodies, were cited as causes of delay.
There is no appeal mechanism and no application tracking, so the applicant cannot see where a file is or why it was returned.
Make the process entirely online with no human intervention in checking documents and drawings; confine officers to site verification, which is their stated responsibility.
Have the system auto-fetch records from other departments (property tax, NOC, layout approvals, colony data) rather than asking the applicant for them again.
Provide an appellate officer and an online grievance route so escalation does not depend on personal relationships.
Make the SLA and deemed approval real, with automatic escalation before the deadline and no reset of the clock when a file is returned.

quotes.speaker: Participant
quotes.quote: Architects approved commercial plots for ten to twelve years. Now the software says only residential, and nothing is in writing.

gaps.text: ED says ABPAS scrutiny happens automatically 'rather than through manual desk review' and holds up MPIDC's digital BPA process as a leading national example; FGD participants directly contradict this in practice, saying 'If the software has already scrutinised it, why do we need manual scrutiny at every level?' and reporting that scanned documents uploaded online are still demanded again in hard copy - corroborating, with concrete specifics, the same gap the ED report's own broader-discussion section already flags.

Participants describe four separate levies (construction, water, development, labour welfare) collected on the same plot but give no amounts, so it is unclear whether or how these overlap with the single ABPAS-generated statutory fee the ED describes.

FGD supplies an informal benchmark the ED interview itself did not state - an 'officer-level SLA' of thirty days - but frames it as an unwritten/unenforced norm, not a displayed rule, and reports it is routinely exceeded per-desk; this fills part of the ED's own MISSING-timeline gap only partially and should not be treated as an official figure.

FGD suggests concrete reforms the ED does not record: fully automate scrutiny with officers confined to site verification, auto-fetch inter-departmental records, publish a fixed document list changeable only by written notification, provide an appellate/grievance officer, and make deemed approval real via auto-escalation that does not reset on a return.

findings.text: Applicants found little guidance online on how to apply for CTE and had to learn the process by asking others who had already been through it.
Even though application and certificate are online, applicants reported needing three to four in-person office visits to complete the CTE process.

No participant across the three CTE sessions was aware of a prescribed or displayed timeline; reported actual experience ranged from about one week to roughly three months for broadly similar applications.
Because requirements are not clearly stated by official sources, applicants engage private consultants - no government-empanelled panel exists - who can expedite the process but add cost.
Queries raised by reviewing officers are often framed in technical/regulatory language that hospital administrative staff must route to a technical person before responding, adding coordination time.

One participant's CTE application took close to three months to clear, with most of the added time in the review/approval stage; a separate, more recent application by a similar applicant was completed in about twenty-one days, entirely online.
A hospital must keep roughly ten to twelve separate licences alive at once (CTE among them), each expiring on its own schedule, requiring a dedicated person just to track renewals.

A delay in one dependent certificate (NABH, received three to four months after assessment) held up the facility's ability to claim an unrelated government scheme benefit (Ayushman), costing roughly three months of lost incentive eligibility.
Multiple departments - police, fire and trade licence among them - inspect the same establishment separately rather than jointly.
The online CTE application form has a word-count limit and the portal reportedly glitches while an application is being filed.
Applicants cannot see which stage an application has reached or with which officer it is lying.

Requirements do not scale with the size of the unit: a small dispensary and a large hospital, or a small and large restaurant, face materially the same CTE requirements, with no explicit scaling by investment, pollution potential or bed count.
Fire, pollution and food-safety regulators each issue separate licences/approvals with separate fees rather than a single combined licence per business type.
Different licences held by the same establishment run on different validity periods, so some renewal is always pending; a licence on a shorter cycle requires a fresh form each time.

Eligibility criteria are not explained before an applicant applies; participants felt the department should state upfront what makes a unit eligible and how to obtain the licence, rather than checking only after submission.
There is no fixed service-level mandate for how many days a raised query or grievance should take to resolve, and training/orientation sessions on regulatory changes are held only infrequently.

At renewal, the same documents submitted at the original CTE stage are required again even where nothing has changed, and a consultant's representative returns to re-verify machinery that was already checked at the first stage.
The same supporting papers are submitted separately to each regulator (fire, pollution, health and safety) rather than collected once and shared between them.
Publish a complete step-by-step application guide with a document checklist on the board's website to reduce dependence on word-of-mouth and consultants.

Create a single window and a single combined licence per business type (fire, pollution and health-and-safety as checklist items within it), make requirements proportionate to investment/scale, and align renewals so they happen together.

gaps.text: No participant in any of the three CTE sessions could state a statutory or displayed timeline; this record relies entirely on experiential estimates (one week to three months) and should not be treated as an official figure.
Fee is described only as 'slab-based on capital investment, auto-generated' with no numeric slabs given across any of the three sessions.

Within the FGD testimony itself, reported CTE processing time ranges from about one week to roughly three months for broadly similar applicants, with one account describing both a three-month delay on an earlier application and a ~21-day turnaround on a more recent one - suggesting inconsistent practice rather than a single reliable benchmark.

Validity period for CTE specifically is not clearly established - participants mention five years for consent 'depending on category' but also describe other licences on shorter cycles, and the two were not clearly distinguished in the discussion.

Participants recommend a single combined licence per business type covering fire, pollution and health-and-safety as checklist items, proportionate (investment/scale-based) requirements, a published timeline, and use of AI to speed up the inspection/scrutiny bottleneck.

remarks: This record is synthesised from three independently held FGD sessions for CTE in MP (Ujjain - healthcare/recycling; Indore - chemical/hospital; Bhopal - mixed), each with distinct participants and dates - these are treated as separate real sessions, not duplicate recordings of one discussion, per the spec's default assumption.
No ED record exists for CTE in Madhya Pradesh to cross-check against; this record is FGD-only and has not been verified against an official source.

findings.text: There is no help desk or reception that can walk a first-time applicant through the CTO process; participants said nobody tells them what to submit, and no manual, format or checklist exists.

Consultants have become a practical necessity rather than a choice - they take the applicant's login credentials, fill the online form and return with the approval, because applicants do not feel they can manage the file themselves.

The portal and its instructions are technical and in English; participants said they can read Hindi comfortably but find the digital language hard to follow, and that Hindi content would remove the need for a consultant.

Participants cannot track an application once filed; one asked the consultant whether tracking exists and was told it does not, leaving applicants to phone the office and, when calls go unanswered, visit in person.
Approval takes anywhere from thirty to sixty days in most accounts, and in one case has still not come after four years, with no explanation given when the office was asked.

Conditions such as an effluent treatment plant (ETP) can turn up midway through processing without being stated anywhere beforehand; one oil-refining participant was required to install an ETP costing about two lakh rupees despite a process that does not use water.
No timeline for deciding a CTO application has been made known to applicants, so there is nothing to hold a long-pending application against.
Category-wise requirements (Red/Orange/Green/White) are not explained to applicants until they are already in the process.
Plant photographs and ETP records have to be sent repeatedly while an application is being processed.
Inspection is a major bottleneck because the regional officer or inspection team has limited availability; staff shortages were specifically cited as a reason applications wait at this stage.
Overall processing was described as around thirty to forty days, with one experience extending to roughly forty to forty-three days.
Online tracking does not remove the need for follow-up; participants said they sometimes have to call officials or visit the office personally when a stage does not move.

Inter-departmental clearances can hold up CTO; Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) permission was cited as a particularly lengthy process for units involving groundwater extraction, with one participant describing a wait of several months.
Information and compliance details already submitted at the CTE stage are required again for CTO, even where there has been no material change.

Participants questioned the need for frequent renewal where the activity and its environmental risk remain substantially unchanged, and suggested longer validity for stable operations and a more direct route for units already ready to operate.
Participants suggested risk- and category-based regulation, with greater reliance on self-compliance and environmental audits to reduce routine inspection visits while retaining oversight.
Participants asked for a transparent fee adjustment/refund mechanism for cases where the validity period granted is shorter than the period for which the fee was paid.
CTO was generally viewed as comparatively simpler than CTE once establishment-stage information and compliance are already in place.

gaps.text: ED states the CTO process has been fully online and faceless since 2011 with 'no physical visit... needed even for scrutiny or certificate collection'; FGD participants across both MP CTO sessions contradict this, reporting no working help desk, no published manual/checklist, and online tracking that 'does not remove the need for follow-up' - one participant said 'I asked the consultant whether any tracking exists and he said there is none,' and others describe having to call or visit the office personally when a stage does not move.

ED gives a statutory ceiling of 30 working days for Red-category CTO (21 for Green/Orange) with actual disposal typically in 15-20 days; FGD participants report typical experience of 30-60 days, a case of 40-43 days, and one case still pending after four years with no explanation given despite being asked - well beyond the ED's stated statutory and practical benchmarks.

ED describes the applicant proposing the pollution-control arrangement (e.g. ETP) as part of the CTO application itself; FGD participants report that such conditions can 'come up during processing' and are 'not stated anywhere beforehand,' with one participant required to install an ETP costing about two lakh rupees despite a process that does not use water.

FGD raises a fee-adjustment scenario the ED record does not address: where the validity period ultimately granted is shorter than the period for which the fee was paid, participants say there is no clear, consistently applied mechanism for adjustment or refund - distinct from the ED's documented treatment of fees on applicant-side rejection.

findings.text: The consumer portal goes down without warning and options present on one screen are missing on the next; participants felt it has stayed in a development stage from the start, with a developer team but no proper testing, so the consumer ends up testing it.

Payment options and receipts do not work reliably: a payment option did not appear for a corporate consumer though it appeared for retail consumers (took developers two to three days to fix), and in another case payment was made but no receipt was generated.
Nothing reaches applicants by email or WhatsApp, there is no single reference number running through the application, and applicants have to ask at each step what happens next.

The application is submitted at the operation and maintenance office, which says the rest lies with the IT cell; the IT cell in turn asks the applicant to sit with the developers, requiring repeated travel (one participant's unit is about 25 km from the office).

A first connection applied for in 2019 took about six months; load enhancement, in the group's experience, takes two to three months; no number of days is communicated and actual time is often about three times what is expected.

Payment options such as an instalment facility are not explained at the counter; one participant made four visits before learning of the instalment option, having been pressed to deposit the full amount.

No revival period is given before or after a connection is declared PDC (permanently disconnected), unlike a bank's ninety-day window before an account is classified non-performing, even when the unit is willing to pay in full.

Authorised contractors are effectively compulsory even for firms with their own licensed electrical engineers; one participant, an electrical engineer with a degree, diploma and licence, said a less-educated contractor can certify his factory while his own sign-off carries no weight.

Contractor classes (A1-A5) determine what work a contractor may perform, but participants said this is applied by practice rather than by circular, differs from district to district, and that Jabalpur has no contractor category at all.
Electricity connection is understood by participants not to fall under the Lok Seva Guarantee Act, so no statutory timeline binds the department as it does for other services with a thirty-day limit.
Subsidies promised jointly by MPEB and MPIDC are left for the industry to chase, because the two bodies have not reconciled the amount between themselves.

Materials such as transformers must be bought only from vendors registered with the electricity company, and are then sent to the department's lab for testing (three to four days), with some material rejected even when sourced from a registered vendor.
Three to four sets of documents already uploaded online must still be submitted again physically after the online application.
Compliance is certified more than once: the electrical inspector's approval is followed by a further declaration through an authorised contractor covering the same compliances a second time.

No officer owns the application end to end; handoffs between the O&M office and the IT cell, each pointing to the other, were cited as a cause of delay, along with objections raised in instalments rather than all together.

Fix and publish a timeline, consider bringing electricity connection under the Lok Seva Guarantee Act, and build auto-escalation so a stage running beyond seven days moves automatically to the next officer.
Make contractor certification optional rather than compulsory, so a firm with its own qualified engineers can certify and proceed without a contractor.
Accept every normal mode of payment (demand draft, RTGS, online) and announce any change in accepted mode by circular before it takes effect.

Participants spoke well of the operation and maintenance team, describing it as helpful, in contrast with other offices such as the electrical inspector's, where they found no one to hear a grievance.

gaps.text: No participant could state a statutory timeline for a new electricity connection or load enhancement; reported figures (about six months for a first connection, two to three months for load enhancement) are experiential, not official, and should not be read as a benchmark the department has committed to.
No specific fee figures were given; the department prepares a cost estimate after application that the consumer must pay, with no breakdown described.

Participants singled out the operation and maintenance (O&M) team as comparatively helpful and responsive, unlike other offices in the same ecosystem (e.g. the electrical inspector's office) where they found no one to hear a grievance.

Recommended reforms: a published, enforceable timeline (potentially under the Lok Seva Guarantee Act) with auto-escalation past seven days per stage, a defined PDC revival window mirroring a bank's ninety-day norm, optional rather than compulsory contractor certification, acceptance of every normal payment mode with changes announced by circular, and regular stakeholder consultations between industry, the department and developers.

Note on a separate file: the FGD quotes table in MP_FGD_BPA.docx (Building Plan Approval) mislabels every row's 'Service Tagged' column as 'Electricity Connection,' apparently a copy-paste/template error from this ECL session's document rather than evidence those quotes concern electricity connection - the content of those quotes (remarks, redundant documents, heritage buildings, architects' authorisation) clearly concerns BPA and has been treated as BPA testimony there.

findings.text: Participants described a strong dependence on private consultants and certified vendors to prepare and submit electrical drawings; one said it is difficult to manage the process without such support.

Although application tracking is available on the portal, users still need to follow up by phone and personal visits, including cases where the concerned inspector/officer was unavailable when they visited.

The portal does not clearly provide a time-bound approval period; reported processing varied considerably - around two to three days in one session, but ten, thirty or even forty days in the other, with cases of one to three months also mentioned.
A shortage of inspectors and licensed electricians was repeatedly highlighted as a bottleneck, linked to infrequent licensing examinations for electricians.

The process can involve a large documentation burden - one session cited roughly forty to fifty documents depending on the case, including layout/location and land-related records, OEM and factory test certificates.
The list of documents required is not published on the website; an experienced contractor knows what is needed, but a new applicant finds it very difficult and faces repeated rejection.
Inspection carries its own separate application and a higher fee - reported at roughly 1.8 to 2 times the drawing-approval fee - with a yearly re-inspection following.

There is no way to track which stage an application has reached or why it was rejected, and no grievance mechanism specific to this service; an appellate officer exists on paper but does not resolve matters in practice.

The approved drawing is not issued with a digital signature on the platform; approval is conveyed by letter/application number over WhatsApp or email, so contractors must print the letter and hand it to the customer or inspector.

There is no module specific to solar installations; the existing format, built around generators, treats the inverter as a generator while the panel is not, which a solar contractor called technically incorrect.
Fees and structure differ from state to state, based on capacity bands (e.g. transformer capacity, cable length), with no all-India standardisation.
No published guidelines on equipment ratings and protection exist against which a drawing can be checked, so a drawing cannot be prepared with confidence it will pass.
There is no integrated or single-window mechanism for related approvals; applicants deal separately with multiple departments and vendors (electrical, fire, boiler, pollution control).

The fee is collected again on resubmission and separately for inspection; the full drawing and document set must be resubmitted afresh after a rejection or for an expansion, even where an earlier approval number exists.
Where an uploaded file is not legible, the department asks for the same documents again by email, effectively duplicating submission.

Drawing approval and inspection are two separate steps: the department informs the applicant once the drawing is approved, inspection is then applied for separately after the work is complete, and the department re-inspects every year.
A healthcare representative reported that yearly inspections arrive without any prior notice; participants asked that hospitals in particular be told in advance.
Publish the document list and technical guidelines (equipment ratings, protection) on the portal, and commit that a drawing prepared to those guidelines will not be rejected.
Issue the approved drawing with a digital signature on the platform itself, so it can be downloaded directly rather than printed from a letter.

Create a government-empanelled pool of certified consultants/contractors with transparent eligibility and fees, conduct electrician licensing exams at least twice a year, and move toward a single-window process across electrical, fire, boiler and pollution-control approvals.

gaps.text: Reported approval timelines are sharply inconsistent even within the FGD evidence itself: one session described a normal two-to-three-day turnaround (occasionally stretching to ten, thirty or forty days), while the other session described a typical range of one-and-a-half to three months - these cannot both be the normal case, and no participant in either session cited an official published timeline to reconcile them against.

Fee is described only in relative terms (inspection roughly 1.8-2 times the drawing-approval fee; fee depends on capacity band and cable length) with no actual fee table or numeric slabs given in either session.
No participant stated a validity period for an approved electrical drawing itself; only the fact of a separate, recurring yearly re-inspection requirement after approval is established.

Recommended reforms: publish the document list and technical guidelines, issue digitally signed approvals online, create a solar-specific drawing module, standardise fees nationally, empanel certified consultants, hold electrician licensing exams more frequently, and move toward a single window across electrical, fire, boiler and pollution-control approvals.

This was a comparatively short, thinner session (five participants, 40 minutes); findings and quotes are fewer in number accordingly, per the spec's guidance not to pad thin sessions.

findings.text: Rural applications still run largely on paper: the file moves from the collector to the SDM, then to the tehsildar and the patwari, with the consultant or client carrying hard copies and chasing each office; participants said the patwari often does not answer the phone.
Hard copies are demanded after applicants have already filled everything in online.

Documents are asked for that the portal itself does not require - for example an electrical NOC insisted on where the portal asks only for an electrical audit, and a CSR report called for as an additional document.

Changes such as a different staircase, a ramp or an emergency exit are sometimes demanded at inspection in a building already constructed to the approved plan, at substantial cost and sometimes requiring structural alteration.

Inspection is delayed where a committee has to be formed and waits until every member is available; one consultant said notice is sometimes given only half an hour before the visit, when the consultant may be two hundred kilometres away.

The portal is tied to a property ID whose linked mobile number does not always match the applicant; where a client holds several plots or has combined two parts of a family property, the process must be repeated for each property ID.
Approvals issued before 2022 were offline and are not on the portal, so a unit with an earlier NOC must apply afresh, paying the fee and going through the full procedure again.
There is no route on the portal through which a grievance is actually resolved.

The compliance checklist offers only yes/no answers with no 'Not Applicable' option, and the same checklist is used for a hospital, a hotel and an industry alike, producing queries on points that do not apply to a given building.
There is no uniform framework for rural applications; practice depends on the collector and the district and keeps changing as officers are transferred every couple of years.

Building classification under the new rules is inconsistent with the National Building Code in at least one instance: a hotel, which the NBC places under residential, is treated by the department as mercantile because it is used for business.

Rural applications require the owner's Samagra ID, which an owner domiciled elsewhere or a government establishment does not have; the NOC then carries the name of whoever the ID belongs to, even after that person leaves.

The portal recognises only a property ID from the urban local body, so tax paid to MPIDC by units in industrial areas is not recognised, and two parts of one family property cannot be given separate building permission (bringing two property IDs and two taxes into one application).

The application goes to the nagar nigam, gram panchayat or nagar palika/parishad depending on the area, with the approved sanction plan, permission letter, land documents and a fire plan prepared by a registered fire consultant in line with Indian Standards and the NBC.

Fire plan approval is valid for two months, linked to the commencement certificate for construction; the fire safety certificate is applied for after construction with an affidavit, electrical safety certificate and the fire plan approval, followed by inspection.
Add a 'Not Applicable' option to the checklist and tailor it to the type of building instead of using the same checklist for a hospital, hotel and industry.
Create a single designated channel for rural applications with a uniform process across districts, rather than leaving practice to change with each transfer.
Stop asking for hard copies of documents already filed online, accept Aadhaar alongside the Samagra ID in rural areas, and let the mobile number against a property ID be updated.
Issue the NOC with a downloadable, verified digital signature, and provide a working helpdesk, an SOP and a genuine grievance route.

gaps.text: No specific fee figure was stated in this session for a fresh Fire NOC; the companion RFNO session names a renewal rate of five rupees per square foot plus a separate inspection fee and says renewal is charged 'at the same rate as the original approval' - which implies but does not confirm the fresh-FNO figure, since this was not independently stated in the FNO session itself.

Participants said that in urban bodies they have not faced significant problems and the thirty-day timeline is generally met, in contrast with the difficulties concentrated in rural areas and MPIDC-held industrial land.

Recommended reforms: a checklist with a 'Not Applicable' option tailored by building type, a single uniform channel for rural applications, acceptance of Aadhaar alongside the Samagra ID, migration of pre-2022 approvals onto the portal, a digitally signed downloadable NOC, and a working helpdesk/SOP/grievance route.

Participants were consistent that difficulties are concentrated in rural areas and in industrial areas where land is held through MPIDC, with urban applications generally working within the stated timeline.

findings.text: The portal limits re-verification applications to six instruments at a time; units with ten to fifteen or more instruments must split a single re-verification exercise into multiple applications, although the concerned officer indicated all instruments should ideally go in one application.

Third-party verification by an authorised vendor adds a separate layer of cost and effort before government stamping and certification; the additional payment is seen as avoidable where direct government verification is possible.
The government fee is visible online, but the third-party verification charge is separate with no clear standard rate, vendor list or service timeline displayed on the portal.
Document upload functionality creates avoidable difficulty around attachment size, format and number of files, including cases where required PDF attachments could not be uploaded.

A fee increase for manufacturer, dealer and retailer licences is expected but has not been notified; participants named this the biggest challenge, since a unit cannot plan a renewal around a figure it does not have, and unconfirmed rumoured figures (fifty thousand for retailers, one lakh for dealers, one and a half lakh for manufacturers) were circulating against a current portal fee of five hundred rupees.
A new entrepreneur cannot tell how many permissions a business needs; this is usually learnt only by asking the department or someone who has already been through the process.
Where documents are submitted physically rather than online, applicants have to visit the office simply to learn whether the file is being checked or is lying untouched.
Participants raised police department involvement in the process as an obstacle, though no specific instance was described.
Participants asked for a transparent framework specifying when third-party verification is mandatory, who is authorised, what charges apply, and how verification is to be carried out.
Land conversion has not become easier despite a stated policy allowing a unit to be set up on any land; panchayat permission alone was reported to take one to two months.
In industrial areas, participants reported paying both the industrial-area authority and the municipal corporation for what amounts to the same property tax/charge.
The online application process itself was described as convenient and time-saving where third-party verification is not involved, with a standard seven-day timeline referred to for processing.

Licences are of three kinds - manufacturer, dealer and repairer - each available as new or renewal, with packaged commodities as a separate category; the licence is valid for five years while weighing instruments must be verified and stamped every year.
Applicants who applied online did so themselves without a consultant and without visiting the office for approval or tracking, receiving status messages through the portal.

Multiple verification records are generated for the same compliance outcome - prior calibration records, a third-party report, then government verification and stamping - and participants questioned whether every step is necessary in every case.
Allow all eligible instruments to be included in a single re-verification application rather than capping it at six.
Publish the authorised third-party vendor framework (vendors, scope, charges, turnaround) on the portal, and integrate the vendor charge into the same online payment as the government fee.
Notify any revised Legal Metrology fee, for new and renewal licences, with its effective date, well before it takes effect, and list every permission a product needs on the portal upfront.
Bring offline/physical file submissions under the same time limit as the online portal route, and make their status visible without requiring an office visit.

gaps.text: Participants themselves describe the anticipated fee increase and its figures (fifty thousand / one lakh / one-and-a-half lakh rupees by category) as unconfirmed rumours, not official information; these are retained only as reported sentiment, not as a factual fee figure, alongside the confirmed current portal fee of five hundred rupees.
No timeline exists for physical/offline file submissions, unlike the seven-day timeline referenced for the online route; participants had no way to estimate when an offline file would be decided.

One session reports the online application route clears 'within the timeline' with no delay, while the other session's dominant theme is uncertainty and delay tied to third-party verification, the six-instrument cap and document-upload failures - these describe two different sub-processes (fresh/renewal licensing vs. re-verification of weighing instruments) rather than a true contradiction, but the overall service experience is uneven depending on which sub-process an applicant needs.

Recommended reforms: remove or raise the six-instrument cap, publish and integrate the third-party verification framework and charges into the online payment flow, announce fee changes with advance notice, list all required permissions upfront for new entrepreneurs, and bring offline submissions under the same timeline and visibility as the online route.

findings.text: Renewal was described as starting almost from scratch in some cases, with applicants having to re-submit documents already available from the earlier CTE/CTO process.
The process is online but applicants still need physical follow-up, including visits to the concerned office and, in some cases, travel to Bhopal.
The portal and compliance requirements are complicated for non-technical applicants; participants said there is no clear manual or easily accessible guidance, increasing dependence on consultants.

Availability of technical/domain experts, particularly for chemical industries, was a major concern; suitable experts may have to be brought in from Gujarat or Maharashtra, increasing both time and cost.
Delays around inspection scheduling and submission of inspection reports, along with staff/manpower constraints at the department, were identified as sources of delay.
Delay was repeatedly linked to business costs - bank interest, labour cost, and resources or land kept tied up - while approval is pending.

There is no government-authorised panel of industry-specific experts and no prescribed or displayed fee structure for them; applicants, especially in chemicals, depend on private consultants whose fees are unregulated and often high.

Expertise for sectors like chemicals is not available near industrial clusters, and departmental officials have limited domain understanding, so applicants bring in experts from Gujarat or Maharashtra.
There is no help desk or user manual to guide applicants on the application, technical terms, documents and the concerned officer, making the process hard for non-technical promoters.
Engagement between the DIC and industries is limited and irregular; some participants had never interacted with the DIC, and there is no forum to raise recurring sector-specific problems.

Reliable testing facilities are not available at the DIC or industrial-area level; applicants rely on private labs charging high, unregulated rates, and heavily loaded labs can take around twenty days to issue reports.
There is no coordination among departments on compliance requests; MSMEs receive repeated, separate requests and visits that take time away from running the business.

Renewal is generally initiated well before expiry - one participant said the application is usually made around six months in advance - but the approval itself may still take around one to two months.

Where a minor document shortfall is identified, participants suggested the renewal process should, where appropriate, continue with a defined period given to submit the additional document rather than stalling entirely.
Explore a shorter, time-bound renewal route, with straightforward cases potentially completed in around fifteen to twenty days.
Create a government-authorised, industry-wise panel of technical experts with a displayed, fixed fee structure, and set up a clear help desk/facilitation centre with FAQs and a simple user manual.

Strengthen local processing and support through DIC/Indore so routine renewal follow-up does not require repeated travel to Bhopal, and improve testing-facility availability with transparent charges at the district/industrial-area level.
Auto-fetch documents already available from the earlier CTE/CTO approval rather than requiring re-upload, and limit updates at renewal to only the information that has actually changed.

gaps.text: ED's documentsNote states Green-category units can avail an auto-renewal facility 'with minimal fresh documentation' and that the same CTO document set 'need not be resubmitted where there is no change'; FGD participants directly contradict this in practice, describing renewal as having 'to be started again from zero' with documents re-uploaded and re-verified even where nothing has changed.

ED records applicantOfficeVisit as 'no' for RCTO, describing the process as fully online/faceless since 2011 with certificate delivery via WhatsApp/SMS requiring no physical visit; FGD participants contradict this, saying 'it's online, but we still have to go to the office,' including travel to Bhopal for routine renewal follow-up.

ED attributes RCTO delay primarily to the applicant's own preparedness (pollution-control proposals not finalised); FGD participants instead emphasise departmental-side causes - inspection scheduling, staff/manpower shortages at the department, and the unavailability of domain experts and testing labs near industrial clusters - as significant, possibly larger, drivers of delay.

Recommended reforms beyond what the ED record covers: a government-authorised, industry-wise expert panel with a displayed fee structure; a help desk/user manual; stronger local (DIC/Indore-level) processing to avoid travel to Bhopal; improved local testing-facility availability; and a defined compliance window for minor document shortfalls instead of stalling the renewal entirely.

findings.text: Renewal needs the same documents as the first application plus a fire audit and the fire plan approval, but the owner rarely keeps the original plan approval, it is not downloadable on the portal, and in some cases the department itself cannot trace it.

Government-sector buildings face the same problem more sharply - in one case (an airport) the plan approval could not be found by anyone, and the consultant could not say where it was to be obtained from.

Approvals issued before 2022 were offline and have not been carried onto the portal, so a unit with an earlier NOC must apply fresh, paying the fee and going through the full procedure again; in some cases there is no physical record either.

Renewal takes longer than the first approval: the first NOC generally comes in thirty days in urban/industrial areas while renewal is allowed sixty days; applicants are told to apply two months before expiry, and a transfer of the SDM can further slow the file.

There is no helpdesk, call centre or manual; when the OTP does not arrive or nothing shows on screen there is nothing to address it except a slow email channel, and no SOP exists for taking up a grievance.
The NOC does not download with a verified signature - signing in to download fails and the certificate carries a mark that its signature is not verified, so it has to be obtained physically.

A lost plan-approval record is treated as the applicant's problem: where the department's own record is lost, the applicant is asked to produce it or start again, although the building itself was approved and built.
No SOP exists for renewal or for taking up grievances; no procedure has been laid down for helping applicants.
Validity periods do not line up across related approvals: building permission runs for five years while the fire safety certificate is valid for three (extendable).

Everything submitted the first time has to be submitted again at renewal, although it is already on the department's record, including the fire plan approval the department itself issued.
Keep plan approvals and earlier NOCs on the portal and downloadable, and bring records from before 2022 onto it.
Provide a working helpdesk and call centre, lay down an SOP for renewal and for grievances, and designate a named officer for follow-up so it does not depend on personal contacts.
Issue the renewed NOC with a verified digital signature so it can be downloaded rather than collected physically.

findings.text: The process still requires physical visits despite an online application, particularly for renewal and for submitting the required receipt/form.
An office visit can take around three to four hours, adding materially to the overall cost of obtaining or renewing the licence.
The online system faces server-related issues that can affect the online process and make it harder to complete the service smoothly.
Renewal is not fully online: approval of a fresh application may be obtained online, but renewal still requires an office visit and physical submission of documents/receipt.
Participants suggested renewal should be fully integrated with the existing website so applicants do not have to visit the office for routine renewal.
Participants indicated the approval process generally takes around seven to fifteen days but felt this timeline should be clearly stated and consistently followed rather than just experienced.
Participants suggested self-inspection could be permitted where appropriate, reducing the need for a separate physical inspection visit.
Documents include basic business and premises records - GST details, rent agreement, and electricity/property-related records - along with the previous receipt where renewal is involved.

The old receipt/document from the previous approval is required again at renewal, suggesting information already available with the department could be used directly through the online system instead.
Server and website issues, and the offline step still required after online application, were cited as the main reasons the process takes longer than it should.
Improve the website and resolve server issues to make the online system more reliable and user-friendly, with the process clearly explained to applicants.
Clearly display the required documents, applicable fee, expected processing time and steps involved on the website before an applicant applies.
Carry forward information already available from the previous licence/receipt instead of requiring the applicant to submit it again.

remarks: Naming-oddity resolution (per spec): Madhya Pradesh's file MP_FGD_TLP.docx uses the code 'TLP,' which is not part of the canonical 26-code legend. The document's own header states the service discussed is 'Trade License Approval (TLP)', and its content - GST/rent/property documents, a seven-to-fifteen-day approval window, and renewal requiring a physical office visit despite an online application - closely matches the trade-licence process described in the companion MP_FGD_TLR.docx (Trade License Renewal) session. This record has therefore been mapped to the canonical code TLA (Trade License - Approval), treating 'TLP' as this state team's own shorthand for the fresh/approval leg of the trade licence process rather than a distinct service; the discrepancy is flagged here rather than inventing a new code.
No ED record exists for Trade License Approval in Madhya Pradesh to cross-check against; this record is FGD-only and has not been verified against an official source.

findings.text: Online payment and server issues during renewal mean the online process does not always progress smoothly, a practical difficulty in completing it.
A physical office visit remains necessary for renewal even though the service is discussed as an online process, reducing the benefit of online submission.

There is uncertainty about whether the same documents must be submitted again at renewal, and whether additional documents or display/print requirements apply in individual cases; the exact document list was not established in the discussion.

A participant described police visits to a hotel premises - checking fire clearance, trade licence, electricity and water connections - followed by additional charges collected without a receipt, with no clarity on the authority for such charges.

The discussion clarified that an exemption being discussed for certain pollution-related requirements/categories should not be understood as a blanket exemption from the trade licence requirement itself.
Participants were encouraged to suggest how the government can make licensing and renewal more predictable and reduce time spent navigating different offices and websites.
No uniform requirement for a fresh inspection at every renewal was established; one participant indicated inspection was not necessarily repeated for renewal.
Participants questioned whether documents already available with the department need to be submitted again at renewal, indicating a need for clearer guidance on what can be carried forward.
Online payment/server problems can interrupt the renewal process and make completion difficult, while needing physical follow-up when the online process does not work smoothly adds further time.
Stabilise the online payment system and ensure the renewal portal and payment gateway work reliably without requiring repeated visits to resolve payment issues.
Enable end-to-end online renewal so applicants do not need to visit the office for routine renewals.
Provide a clear, service-specific document checklist for renewal, stating exactly what is required and what, once valid, need not be submitted again.

Strengthen single-window integration across licensing services, and clarify the role and authority of agencies conducting inspections at business premises so any additional charge is supported by an official receipt.
Use WhatsApp or a similar official messaging channel to communicate renewal-related instructions, updates and requirements directly to applicants.
